The meanings that stories provide are not derived from the individual meanings of the events they represent, rather the individual events derive their meaning from the overall meaning of the story. The outcome of the story determines the meaning of the events within the story. Why something happened is explained by the end of the story in which it happened. But this is ascribed by the agent, that individual. The difficulty arises in understanding how mental states are related to events, whether emotional, causal or something else. The divergence not only has implications for ways in which we identify material objects persisting across space and time, but also with respect to moral attributions of praise and blame. These uniquely belong to active *immaterial* objects such as persons.

Kantians and Utilitarians have differing conceptions of agency which together represent a source of justification for either view. When concerning moral obligation and duty for instance, it is the moral agent who deserves to be praised or blamed. In this way, say my acceptance of a person's human rights, has nothing to do with me. Utilitarians on the other hand ask 'what should be done for the agent?', persons with a characteristic form of experience and the Kantian asks 'what ought the agent do?', despite a given experience. Parfit's account does not account for what we all might think of as the exercise of agency. As such, Korsgaard goes on to argue that focusing on what an agent does, rather than their experiences, will lead to a drastically different concept of identity, one that is grounded in a unique characterization of agency. She calls this characterization 'practical' identity.

Korsgaard then, defends a concept of narrative identity. Reductionist and causalist conceptions of identity undermine what we think of as agency with regard to moral responsibility. These accounts fail to explain the attribution of praise or blame in response to an agent's actions. They offer no way to define the line as beginning at *T$_1$* and ending at *T$_2$*. On this account, the object, that persistent thing deserving of either moral praise or blame, is indefinable.

On her narrative account of identity, a person is an agent who uses narrative to define her own constitution. She calls this the *self*-constitution model of personal identity. As such, Korsgaard defends an account of personhood and identity grounded in narrative agency. On this account, we are defined by the stories we accept about ourselves. The act of acceptance means that we select individual events from our pasts in order to construct a narrative that defines us.

As an explanation, narrative theories provide one account of personhood by explaining the relationship of cause and event in a way that preserves agency. Stories make our lives intelligible [@vell03] by providing motive and context to a collection of events and episodes. In other words, narrative gives meaning to otherwise meaningless events. Overall, the meanings that stories provide are not derived from the individual meanings of the events they represent. The individual events derive their meaning from the overall meaning of the story and the outcome of the story determines the meaning of the events within the story. Finally, the meaning of the outcome is determined by the story teller. Why something happened is explained by the end of the story in which it happened.

The second question is even more difficult and grounds the first. It begins as a question about ourselves and the sources of our beliefs as to what is possible. Peter @gold09 convincingly argues that we would not experience regret for an event that we had no control over the same way we would for an event we did have control over. It will first be helpful to understand how narrative theories shape our identities.
